river:丽水.note: Nanzhao set up the Lishui military governorship on its upper reaches.

river:汾水.note: The central axis of Hedong: Taiyuan, Jinzhou and Jiangzhou all stand on the Fen River.

river:郁水.note: The main river of Lingnan, flowing past Wuzhou and Duanzhou to Guangzhou.

river:泸水.note: Called the Lu River under the Tang; one of the boundaries between Nanzhao and Xichuan.

river:江.note: The Great River. In the later Tang the Jiang–Huai region became the foundation of state revenue.

river:汉水.note: Also called the Mian River; Xiangzhou was the key city on its middle course.

river:娑陵水.note: Grazing lands of the Uyghurs and the Yenisei Kyrgyz.

river:富良江.note: The principal river of Annan; Giao Châu stands on its right bank.

river:大渡水.note: A natural boundary separating Xichuan from Nanzhao and Tibet.

river:潢水.note: Homeland of the Khitans; the Liao Supreme Capital stood north of it.

river:汶江.note: The water source of the Chengdu Plain; the Dujiangyan weir is on this river.

river:兰沧水.note: The great river of western Nanzhao.

river:桑干河.note: Runs between Daibei and Youzhou; under the Tang its lower course was called the Lugou River.

river:臧河.note: The Yarlung valley, where the Tibetan Empire arose, lies on its south bank.

river:黔江.note: Called the Fuling River or Qian River under the Tang.

river:淮水.note: The Huai River. Until 958 the Later Zhou and the Southern Tang were divided by the Huai; afterwards by the Yangtze. Under the Tang and the Northern Song the Huai flowed past Sizhou and Chuzhou to the sea on its own (after the Yellow River took over the Huai in 1194, its lower course silted up and Hongze Lake formed).

river:闽江.note: Formed where the Jianxi and Futunxi meet, it flows past Fuzhou to the sea.

river:嘉陵江.note: Also called the Western Han River; one of the roads into Shu ran along it.

river:溱水.note: Flows south past Shaozhou to Guangzhou; the river section of the Dayu Pass route.

river:河.note: Under the Tang and Song the lower Yellow River roughly followed the channel trained by Wang Jing in the Eastern Han, passing Huazhou, Chanzhou, north of Yunzhou and north of Qizhou, and reaching the sea through Dizhou and Binzhou. The modern lower Yellow River (dashed) took over the course of the Daqing River to the sea after the river shifted at Tongwaxiang in 1855.

river:鸭渌水.note: The Yalu route, Balhae's tribute road, ran along the river.

river:黑水.note: The Heishui Mohe lived on its lower course.

river:望建河.note: The Mengwu Shiwei lived to its east.

river:渭水.note: The lifeline of Guanzhong; grain boats reached Chang'an by the Wei River and the Cao Canal.

river:泾水.note: The Jingyuan fanzhen took its name from this river.

river:漳水.note: Flows through the area of Xiangzhou and Weizhou.

river:嗢昆水.note: Site of the Uyghur khagan's camp.

river:济水（清河）.mod: the ancient Ji River (most of today's lower Yellow River follows its old course)
river:济水（清河）.note: Under the Tang the Ji River flowed northeast from Daye Marsh past Yunzhou, Qizhou, Zizhou and Qingzhou to the sea, and was also called the Qing River; the Shandong section of today's Yellow River took over its old course.

river:洛水.note: Luoyang, the Eastern Capital, straddles the Luo River.

river:洛水（北）.note: Flows through Fuzhou, Fangzhou and Tongzhou.

river:颍水.note: Flows through Xuzhou, Chenzhou and Yingzhou into the Huai.

river:泗水.note: Flows through Yanzhou, Xuzhou and Sizhou into the Huai; Xuzhou stands where the Si and the Bian meet.

river:滹沱河.note: Flows south of the city of Zhenzhou; the Surrender at Zhongdu Bridge in 946 took place on this river.

river:淯水.note: The main river of the Nanyang Basin, joining the Han at Xiangzhou.

river:资水.note: Flows past Shaozhou into Dongting Lake.

river:漓水.note: Linked to the Xiang River by the Lingqu Canal.

river:弱水.note: Flows past Ganzhou and north into Juyan Lake.

river:破釜塘.mod: Hongze Lake (the present lake formed later)
river:破釜塘.note: Under the Tang there were only small lakes here on the south bank of the Huai, such as Pofu Reservoir and Baishui Reservoir. Today's Hongze Lake formed in the Ming and Qing, and the city of Sizhou lies at the bottom of the lake.

river:湄沱湖.note: Source of the famous Balhae product, "the crucian carp of Lake Meituo".

river:太湖.note: Known in antiquity as Zhenze and Juqu.

river:柏海@鄂陵湖.note: In 641, when Princess Wencheng went to Tibet, Songtsen Gampo came to meet her at Baihai Lake.

river:热海.note: Xuanzang called it the "Great Clear Lake".

river:青海.note: Contested by Tang and Tibet; former land of the Tuyuhun.

river:大野泽.note: Called Juye Marsh under the Tang. After the Yellow River broke its banks at Huazhou in 944, it merged with the Wen and Ji rivers to form Liangshan Marsh.

river:居延海.mod: Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia (today's Juyan Lake)
river:居延海.note: The terminal lake of the Ruoshui; the Tang stationed Ningkou Jun here.

river:滇池.note: Nanzhao's Tuodong City stood by Lake Dian.

river:洱海.note: Known in antiquity as the Western Er River; the heartland of Nanzhao.

canal:通济渠（汴河）.mod: Tongji Canal section of the Sui–Tang Grand Canal
canal:通济渠（汴河）.note: Dug under Emperor Yang of Sui to link the Yellow River and the Huai, it was the lifeline of grain transport under the Tang and Song. Bianzhou, Songzhou, Suzhou and Sizhou grew up along it, and the Five Dynasties (except the Later Tang) and the Northern Song made Kaifeng their capital because of the easy transport the Bian River offered.

canal:永济渠（御河）.note: Ran from the mouth of the Qin River north to Zhuo Commandery (Youzhou); dug when the Sui attacked Goguryeo. The Hebei fanzhen of the Tang also used it for transport.

canal:山阳渎（邗沟）.note: From Yangzhou to Chuzhou, linking the Yangtze and the Huai.

canal:江南河.note: From Runzhou to Hangzhou; the revenue of Jiangnan was shipped north along it.

canal:漕渠.mod: from Xi'an to Tongguan, Shaanxi (course of the Sui Guangtong Canal, long silted up)
canal:漕渠.note: A transport canal from Chang'an to Tong Pass, running parallel to the Wei River.

canal:灵渠.note: Dug under the Qin to link the Xiang and Li rivers; rebuilt by Li Bo in 825 and by Yu Mengwei in 868.

range:终南山（秦岭）.note: The southern screen of Guanzhong; the Tang called it the Southern Mountains or Zhongnan Mountains. The Ziwu, Tangluo, Baoxie and Chencang valley roads cross it to Hanzhong.

range:巴山.note: The barrier between Hanzhong and Ba–Shu, crossed by the Micang and Lizhi roads.

range:太行山.note: The divide between Hedong and Hebei, crossed by the "Eight Passes of the Taihang". In the late Tang Li Keyong held Hedong and Zhu Quanzhong southern Hebei, and the two fought back and forth along the Taihang.

range:吕梁山.note: The mountains of western Hedong, bordered on the west by the Yellow River.

range:中条山.note: South of Hezhong; the salt lake lies at its northern foot.

range:恒山.note: The Northern Sacred Peak. Under the Tang the Northern Peak was Mount Damao, northwest of Quyang, and the sacrifices were made at the Temple of the Northern Peak in Quyang.

range:五台山.note: The seat of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, a Buddhist holy site under the Tang.

range:燕山.note: The northern barrier of Youzhou, where Juyong Pass, Gubeikou and Songting Pass lie. With the cession of the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun, the Central Plains lost this line.

range:阴山.note: The barrier between the steppe south of the Gobi and the Ordos Loop; the three Shouxiang Cities guarded its southern foot.

range:陇山.note: The barrier between Guanzhong and Longyou; after Tibet took Longyou it became the Tang–Tibetan front.

range:祁连山.note: On the south side of the Hexi Corridor; the Tang also called it the Southern Mountains or Snow Mountains.

range:阿尔金山.note: Between the Southern Route of the Western Regions and Qinghai; in the Five Dynasties the Zhongyun tribe lived here.

range:昆仑山.note: The southern mountains of Khotan, a source of jade.

range:积石山.note: Called the Great Jishi Mountains under the Tang; the Yellow River bends around them.

range:唐古拉山.note: The old Tang–Tibet road crossed these mountains into northern Tibet. The name is modern.

range:冈底斯山.note: The northern edge of the valleys of southern Tibet. The name is modern.

range:雪山.note: The great snow mountains separating Tibet from India and Nepal.

range:葱岭.note: The divide between the Western Regions and Central Asia; the Tang set up the Congling Garrison here.

range:天山.note: The Tang called it the Tian Shan or the White Mountains; its eastern section was also called the Zheluoman Mountains. Beiting lay to the north, Anxi to the south.

range:金山.note: The Karluks originally lived southwest of the Altai Mountains.

range:燕然山.note: In the heart of the lands north of the Gobi; the Uyghur khagan's camp lay at its eastern foot.

range:大兴安岭.note: Separating the Shiwei and the Khitans from the tribes north of the Gobi. The name is modern.

range:太白山.note: Called the Taibai or Tutai Mountains under the Tang; a famous mountain in Balhae.

range:医巫闾山.note: A famous mountain of Liaoxi, where Yelü Bei, King of Dongdan under the Liao, kept his library.

range:泰山.note: The Eastern Sacred Peak, where Emperor Xuanzong performed the feng and shan sacrifices in 725.

range:华山.note: The Western Sacred Peak, west of Tong Pass.

range:嵩山.note: The Central Sacred Peak, where Wu Zetian once performed the feng and shan sacrifices.

range:伏牛山.note: Between Luoyang and the Nanyang Basin.

range:巫山.note: Site of the Three Gorges of the Yangtze.

range:武陵山.note: Home of the Five Streams tribes.

range:雪峰山.note: Between the Zi and Yuan rivers. The name is modern.

range:五岭.note: The Five Ridges (Yuecheng, Dupang, Mengzhu, Qitian and Dayu), dividing Lingnan from the Central Plains.

range:罗霄山.note: Between Hunan and Jiangxi. The name is modern.

range:武夷山.note: Between Fujian and Jiangxi; the western screen of Min.

range:仙霞岭.note: In 878 Huang Chao cut a mountain road of seven hundred li through here into Fujian.

range:庐山.note: Also called Kuanglu; Bai Juyi built a thatched hall here.

range:岷山.note: In northern Xichuan; after Tibet took Songzhou it marked the Tang–Tibetan border.

range:邛崃山.note: The western edge of the Chengdu Plain; the Tang called it the Western Mountains, and it bordered Tibet.

range:大雪山.note: The eastern edge of the western Sichuan plateau. The name is modern.

range:点苍山.note: On the west shore of Erhai Lake; Tang and Nanzhao concluded the Treaty of Diancang here in 794.

range:哀牢山.note: Southeast of the Nanzhao heartland. The name is modern.

desert:大流沙.note: The great desert between the southern and northern routes of the Western Regions.

desert:大碛.note: The Gobi between the lands south and north of the desert, which the Tang called the Great Desert or the Sandy Desert.

desert:普纳沙.note: Around Xiazhou (Tongwan City); desertification was already evident under the Tang.

capital:长安.note: The Tang capital, also called Shangdu (the Upper Capital) or the Western Capital. Its outer walls ran about 36 km (sixty-seven li) around, it had 108 wards, and its population was nearly a million. It fell many times, in 756, 763, 783, 880 and later. In 904 Zhu Quanzhong forced Emperor Zhaozong to move to Luoyang and pulled down the palaces, and Chang'an was never a capital again.

capital:洛阳（东都）.note: The Tang Eastern Capital. In 904 Emperor Zhaozong was moved to Luoyang by Zhu Quanzhong and murdered there the same year; in 907 Emperor Ai abdicated here.

capital:凤翔（西京）.note: In the 2nd month of 757 Emperor Suzong moved from Pengyuan to Fengxiang, and made it his temporary capital; in the 9th month he sent out from here the army that retook Chang'an, and in the 12th month Fengxiang was named the Western Capital.

capital:成都（南京）.note: Emperor Xuanzong fled to Shu in 756; in the 12th month of 757 Chengdu was made the Southern Capital. At the end of 880 Emperor Xizong, fleeing Huang Chao, again took the court to Chengdu, returning to the capital in 885.

capital:奉天.note: After the Jingyuan mutiny in the 10th month of 783, Emperor Dezong fled to Fengtian, where Zhu Ci besieged him for over a month.

capital:兴元（梁州）.note: When Li Huaiguang rebelled in the 2nd month of 784, Emperor Dezong fled again, to Liangzhou; in the 6th month he raised Liangzhou to Xingyuan Fu, and in the 7th month he returned to Chang'an.

capital:洛阳（燕都）.note: An Lushan proclaimed himself emperor at Luoyang in the 1st month of 756, and the Tang army recovered it in the 10th month of 757; Shi Siming took Luoyang again in the 9th month of 759, and the Yan army held it until the Tang army recovered it once more in the 10th month of 762 (Shi Siming made Fanyang his Yan capital, and Shi Chaoyi made Luoyang his capital).

capital:长安（朱泚）.note: Zhu Ci held Chang'an as emperor for eight months.

capital:汴州（大楚）.note: Li Xilie took Bianzhou at the end of 783, proclaimed himself emperor in the 1st month of 784, and was driven back to Caizhou in the 11th month of the same year.

capital:长安（大齐）.note: Huang Chao took the throne in the Hanyuan Hall and held Chang'an for over two years.

capital:开封（东都）.note: Zhu Quanzhong raised Bianzhou to Kaifeng Fu and called it the Eastern Capital, with Luoyang as the Western Capital. In 909 he moved to Luoyang; in 913 the last Liang emperor moved the capital back to Kaifeng.

capital:洛阳（西都）.note: The Later Liang made Luoyang its capital for a time (909–913).

capital:太原（晋王府）.old: Taiyuan (seat of the Prince of Jin)
capital:太原（晋王府）.note: Seat of the Princes of Jin, Li Keyong and his son Li Cunxu; the city of Jinyang was the foundation of their power in Hedong.

capital:凤翔（岐王府）.old: Fengxiang (seat of the Prince of Qi)
capital:凤翔（岐王府）.note: Li Maozhen set up his court as Prince of Qi, with Fengxiang as its seat.

capital:幽州（燕都）.note: Liu Shouguang proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan at Youzhou in 911.

capital:镇州（赵王府）.old: Zhenzhou (seat of the Prince of Zhao)
capital:镇州（赵王府）.note: Seat of Wang Rong, Prince of Zhao.

capital:成都（前蜀）.note: Capital of the Former Shu. Wang Jian's tomb (Yongling) is within today's city of Chengdu.

capital:洛阳（后唐）.note: The Later Tang made Luoyang its capital (Luojing), with Weizhou as the Eastern Capital (Xingtang Fu) and Taiyuan as the Northern Capital.

capital:开封（东京）@938.note: The Later Jin moved its capital to Kaifeng in 938 and called it the Eastern Capital, Kaifeng Fu; the Later Han, the Later Zhou and the Northern Song all had their capitals here afterwards.

capital:太原（后汉起兵）.note: Liu Zhiyuan proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan in the 2nd month of 947 and entered Kaifeng in the 6th month.

capital:开封（后周）.note: Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou enlarged the outer city of Kaifeng in 955, setting the scale of the Northern Song Eastern Capital.

capital:开封（东京）@960.note: Capital of the Northern Song, the Eastern Capital Kaifeng Fu, with Luoyang as the Western Capital.

capital:太原（北汉）.note: Jinyang, capital of the Northern Han; burned after the Song destroyed the Northern Han in 979.

capital:广陵（江都）.note: Capital of Wu under the Yang family; Yangzhou was raised to Jiangdu Fu in 919.

capital:金陵（江宁）.note: Capital of the Southern Tang, Jiangning Fu (the Western Capital).

capital:南昌（南都）.note: In 961 Li Jing, the second ruler of the Southern Tang, moved the capital to Nanchang Fu, called the Southern Capital, and died the same year; the last ruler, Li Yu, moved the capital back to Jinling.

capital:杭州（西府）.note: Capital of Wuyue; Qian Liu enlarged its outer walls, and it was known as a "heavenly palace on earth".

capital:福州（长乐府）.note: Capital of Min; raised to Changle Fu in 933.

capital:长沙.note: Capital of Chu under the Ma family (seat of the Tiance Mansion).

capital:兴王府（广州）.note: Capital of the Southern Han, where Liu Yan built lavish palaces.

capital:江陵.note: Seat of the Gao family of Jingnan.

capital:成都（后蜀）.note: Capital of the Later Shu. Meng Chang planted hibiscus all over the city, which is why Chengdu is called the "City of Hibiscus".

capital:逻些.note: Capital of the Tibetan Empire; the Tang–Tibet Treaty Pillar (823) stands in front of the Jokhang Temple.

capital:斡耳朵八里.note: The city of the Uyghur khagan's camp (Ordu-Baliq) on the Orkhon River, with the stele of the Khagan of the Nine-Clan Uyghurs. Burned by the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 840.

capital:太和城.note: The early capital of Nanzhao, where the Nanzhao Dehua Stele (766) stands.

capital:阳苴咩城@779.note: Nanzhao moved its capital here in 779; it was later the capital of Dachanghe and of the Dali Kingdom.

capital:阳苴咩城@902.note: The capital of the Zheng family's Dachanghe, the Zhao family's Datianxing and the Yang family's Dayining.

capital:上京龙泉府.note: Capital of Balhae, laid out on the model of Chang'an; its outer wall is 16 km around.

capital:东京龙原府.note: Balhae moved its capital to the Eastern Capital for a time (785–794).

capital:中京显德府.note: Balhae's capital in its early period.

capital:忽汗城（天福城）.note: After destroying Balhae, the Khitans renamed Huhan City Tianfu City and made it the capital of Dongdan.

capital:东平（辽阳）.note: In 928 Dongdan moved south to Liaodong and made Dongping its Southern Capital.

capital:潢水牙帐 · 上京.note: Site of the Khitan khagan's camp. In 918 Yelü Abaoji built Huangdu, which was renamed the Supreme Capital, Linhuang Fu, in 938.

capital:奚王牙帐.note: The Xi king's camp; the Liao Central Capital, Dading Fu, was later built here.

capital:金城.note: Royal capital of Silla; the Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto were built in the mid-8th century.

capital:完山州.note: Capital of Gyeon Hwon's Later Baekje.

capital:平安京.note: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital here in 794, laying it out on the model of Tang Chang'an.

capital:高昌.note: Winter capital of the Qocho Uyghurs, who spent the summer at Beiting.

capital:甘州.note: Camp of the Ganzhou Uyghur khagan.

capital:于阗.note: The Western City, the capital of Khotan.

capital:八剌沙衮.note: Seat of the Kara-Khanid great khagan; with Kashgar, the seat of the junior khagan, it was one of the khanate's two capitals.

capital:沙州.note: Seat of the military governor of Guiyi Jun.

capital:夏州.note: Seat of Dingnan Jun, on the site of Tongwan City of the Great Xia of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

capital:古螺.note: Ngô Quyền proclaimed himself king in 939, with his capital at Cổ Loa.

capital:华闾.note: Capital of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh's Đại Cồ Việt.

capital:因陀罗补罗.mod: Đồng Dương, Da Nang (formerly Quảng Nam province), Vietnam

battle:常山之战.note: Yan Gaoqing, governor of Changshan Commandery, rose with his younger cousin Yan Zhenqing, governor of Pingyuan; seventeen commanderies of Hebei answered them, cutting An Lushan's line of retreat. Shi Siming turned back and took Changshan; Yan Gaoqing was taken to Luoyang and died cursing the rebels (Wen Tianxiang's "Song of the Righteous Spirit": "the tongue of Yan of Changshan").

battle:潼关之战.note: Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guozhong pressed Geshu Han to leave the pass and fight a decisive battle; 200,000 Tang troops were ambushed and routed on the Xiyuan plain at Lingbao, Geshu Han was seized by his own officers and handed over to Yan, and Tong Pass fell. Xuanzong abandoned Chang'an and fled, and on the way came the Mawei Station incident.

battle:睢阳之战.cmd: Yin Ziqi vs. Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan
battle:睢阳之战.note: Zhang Xun first held Yongqiu, then with Xu Yuan held Suiyang to the death for ten months with fewer than 10,000 men against more than 100,000 Yan troops, until the food ran out, the city fell and they were killed. Suiyang shielded the Jiang–Huai region and so saved the Tang's source of revenue; ten days after it fell the Tang army recovered Luoyang.

battle:太原之战@757.cmd: Li Guangbi vs. Shi Siming and Cai Xide
battle:太原之战@757.note: Li Guangbi held Taiyuan with fewer than 10,000 men, digging trenches and tunnels and building trebuchets; he held out for more than fifty days and killed over 70,000 Yan troops, and Shi Siming withdrew.

battle:香积寺之战.sides: Tang and the Uyghurs defeated Yan
battle:香积寺之战.cmd: Li Chu, Guo Ziyi and the Uyghur yabghu vs. An Shouzhong and Li Guiren
battle:香积寺之战.note: 150,000 Tang troops and 4,000 Uyghur horsemen fought the decisive battle north of Xiangji Temple, south of Chang'an. The Uyghurs circled round to strike the Yan rear, the Yan army collapsed and 60,000 were beheaded; Chang'an was recovered the next day.

battle:新店之战.sides: Tang and the Uyghurs defeated Yan
battle:新店之战.note: Uyghur horsemen came from behind the southern hills to catch the Yan army in a pincer; the Yan army was routed, An Qingxu abandoned Luoyang and fled north to Yecheng, and the Tang recovered the Eastern Capital.

battle:邺城之战.cmd: nine military governors (Guo Ziyi, Li Guangbi and others) vs. Shi Siming and An Qingxu
battle:邺城之战.note: Emperor Suzong appointed no supreme commander and made the eunuch Yu Chao'en army supervisor instead; 600,000 Tang troops besieged Yecheng for half a year without taking it. Shi Siming came to the rescue; while the armies were fighting a violent storm blew up and the Tang army scattered. Shi Siming then killed An Qingxu and proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan. Du Fu's "Three Officers" and "Three Partings" describe the conscription around this campaign.

battle:邙山之战.cmd: Shi Siming vs. Li Guangbi and Pugu Huai'en
battle:邙山之战.note: Pressed by Yu Chao'en to give battle, the Tang army was badly beaten at Mount Mang, and Heyang and Huaizhou were lost again. In the same year Shi Siming was killed by his son Shi Chaoyi.

battle:吐蕃陷长安.cmd: Tibet vs. Emperor Daizong of Tang
battle:吐蕃陷长安.note: 200,000 Tibetans advanced east; Emperor Daizong fled to Shanzhou, and the Tibetans entered Chang'an and set up Li Chenghong, Prince of Guangwu, as emperor. Fifteen days later Guo Ziyi recovered the city.

battle:泾阳之盟.sides: Tang and the Uyghurs defeated Tibet
battle:泾阳之盟.note: Pugu Huai'en rebelled against the Tang and led 300,000 Tibetans, Uyghurs and others in an invasion, but died of illness on the way. Guo Ziyi took off his helmet and rode alone into the Uyghur camp to renew the old friendship; together with the Uyghurs he attacked the Tibetans on the Xiyuan plain at Lingtai, and Guanzhong was relieved.

battle:洹水之战.cmd: Ma Sui, Li Baozhen and Li Peng vs. Tian Yue
battle:洹水之战.note: In the Jianzhong war to curb the fanzhen the Tang army routed Tian Yue on the Huan River and besieged Weizhou; then Zhu Tao and Wang Wujun changed sides, four fanzhen joined forces and their leaders proclaimed themselves kings, and the war turned.

battle:奉天之围.cmd: Emperor Dezong of Tang and Hun Jian vs. Zhu Ci
battle:奉天之围.note: After the Jingyuan mutiny Emperor Dezong fled to Fengtian; Zhu Ci led a great army in person and besieged the city for more than a month. Hun Jian held it to the end, and Li Huaiguang hurried back from Hebei to break the siege. Lu Zhi drafted for Dezong the "Great Amnesty on Changing the Reign Title at Fengtian", the "edict of self-reproach".

battle:李晟收复长安.note: Li Sheng camped with an isolated army at the East Wei Bridge and refused to be absorbed by Li Huaiguang; in the 5th month he broke into Chang'an through the Guangtai Gate, and Zhu Ci fled west and was killed.

battle:平凉劫盟.note: The Tibetan chief minister Shang Jiezan pretended to make a treaty and had hidden troops seize and kill the Tang envoys; Hun Jian barely escaped with his life, and the deputy envoy Cui Hanheng and more than sixty others were captured.

battle:北庭之战.sides: Tibet defeated Tang and the Uyghurs
battle:北庭之战.cmd: Tibet and the Karluks vs. Yang Xigu and Jiegan Jiasi
battle:北庭之战.note: Tibet, joined by the Karluks and the White-Clad Turks, attacked Beiting; the Uyghur chief minister Jiegan Jiasi failed to relieve it, Beiting fell, and its military governor Yang Xigu fled to Xizhou and was later killed by the Uyghurs.

battle:维州之战.note: Wei Gao, allied with Nanzhao and the Eastern tribes, attacked in nine columns and routed the Tibetans around Yazhou and Weizhou, capturing the Tibetan inner chief minister Lun Mangre. From then on Tibet declined.

battle:鹿头关之战.note: The first campaign after Emperor Xianzong's accession: Gao Chongwen won eight battles out of eight, broke through Lutou Pass, took Chengdu and captured Liu Pi.

battle:蔡州之战.note: The war in Huaixi had dragged on for three years. Li Su treated the surrendered officer Li You generously, then on a snowy night made a forced march of seventy li to surprise Caizhou and captured Wu Yuanji alive. Huaixi, held independently for more than thirty years, was pacified, and the Hebei fanzhen were struck with fear.

battle:平淄青.cmd: Tian Hongzheng, Li Guangyan and others vs. Li Shidao
battle:平淄青.note: Troops from many fanzhen joined the attack; Liu Wu, Ziqing's chief commander of troops, turned his army back and beheaded Li Shidao and his son. The twelve prefectures were pacified and divided into three fanzhen.

battle:杀胡山之战.cmd: Liu Mian and Shi Xiong vs. Wujie Khagan
battle:杀胡山之战.note: After the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate, Wujie Khagan came south to raid the frontier, holding Princess Taihe, given to the Uyghurs in a marriage alliance; Shi Xiong raided his camp by night and brought Princess Taihe back, and Wujie fled far away.

battle:泽潞之役.note: Liu Zhen of Zhaoyi defied the court and set himself up; the chief minister Li Deyu insisted on a punitive campaign and had Chengde and Weibo send troops. In 844 Liu Zhen was killed by his officer Guo Yi, and Zhaoyi was pacified.

battle:沙州起义.note: Zhang Yichao led Chinese and Tibetan inhabitants in a rising, drove out the Tibetan commanders and recovered Shazhou and Guazhou, then fought his way across Hexi; in 851 he sent envoys with the maps and registers of eleven prefectures to submit to the Tang.

battle:交趾之战.cmd: Gao Pian vs. Yang Sijin of Nanzhao
battle:交趾之战.note: Nanzhao took Jiaozhi twice (the second time in 863), killing or carrying off nearly 150,000 people in all. Gao Pian counterattacked from 864, recovered Jiaozhi in 866 and built the citadel of Đại La; Annan was reorganized as the Jinghai Jun.

battle:庞勋之乱.cmd: Kang Chengxun and Zhuye Chixin of the Shatuo vs. Pang Xun
battle:庞勋之乱.note: Eight hundred Xuzhou soldiers garrisoning Guizhou marched home north without orders, seized Xuzhou and grew to 200,000 men; the Tang put them down with the help of Shatuo cavalry, and Zhuye Chixin was rewarded with the name Li Guochang. As historians put it, "The Tang fell to Huang Chao, but the root of the disaster lay in Guilin."

battle:成都之围.cmd: Yan Qingfu and others vs. Shilong of Nanzhao
battle:成都之围.note: Nanzhao invaded Xichuan in force and besieged Chengdu; the soldiers and people in the city held out until relief arrived and Nanzhao withdrew. Gao Pian took up his post in 875 and built Chengdu's outer wall.

battle:黄巢陷广州.note: Huang Chao came south and took Guangzhou; according to Arabic sources he killed great numbers of foreign merchants. Epidemics were raging in Lingnan, and Huang Chao soon turned north.

battle:黄巢破潼关.old: Huang Chao breaks through Tong Pass
battle:黄巢破潼关.note: Huang Chao's 600,000 men broke through Tong Pass; Emperor Xizong fled to Chengdu and Huang Chao entered Chang'an.

battle:梁田陂之战.mod: west of Huazhou District, Weinan, Shaanxi
battle:梁田陂之战.note: Li Keyong with his Shatuo "Raven Army" routed 150,000 of Huang Chao's troops, and in the 4th month recovered Chang'an. He was twenty-eight, and his name was known throughout the land.

battle:狼虎谷.note: Defeated in Langhu Valley on Mount Tai, Huang Chao was killed by his nephew Lin Yan (one account says he killed himself), ending a rising that had lasted ten years.

battle:上源驿之变.note: Returning from the pursuit of Huang Chao, Li Keyong passed through Bianzhou; Zhu Quanzhong gave a banquet for him at the Shangyuan Post Station, then at night sent troops to attack him, and Li Keyong escaped by letting himself down the city wall on a rope. From then on Zhu and Li were sworn enemies, and their feud shaped the wars of the north for the next forty years.

battle:清口之战.cmd: Yang Xingmi and Zhu Jin vs. Pang Shigu
battle:清口之战.note: Zhu Quanzhong attacked Huainan in two columns; Yang Xingmi broke the Huai dikes to flood Pang Shigu's camp and killed Pang Shigu, and the Bianzhou army was routed; the other column under Ge Congzhou withdrew on hearing the news. This settled the division between north and south.

battle:凤翔之围.note: The eunuch Han Quanhui carried Emperor Zhaozong off to Li Maozhen. Zhu Quanzhong besieged Fengxiang for a year, until people in the city were eating one another and Li Maozhen killed the eunuchs and handed over Zhaozong. From then on Zhu Quanzhong controlled the court.

battle:潞州之战.note: The Liang army built a double-walled siege camp and besieged Luzhou for a year. Li Keyong had just died; Li Cunxu used a thick fog to strike the siege camp from Sanchui Ridge and routed the Liang army. Zhu Quanzhong sighed, "A son should be like Li Yazi."

battle:柏乡之战.sides: Jin and Zhao defeated Later Liang
battle:柏乡之战.cmd: Li Cunxu and Zhou Dewei vs. Wang Jingren
battle:柏乡之战.note: The Jin army harassed the enemy with cavalry and counterattacked once the enemy was worn out; Liang's best troops were almost entirely destroyed, and the Hebei fanzhen went over to Jin.

battle:幽州之围.note: The Khitans, said to number 300,000, besieged Youzhou for more than two hundred days; Li Siyuan and Li Cunshen relieved it with 70,000 foot and horse.

battle:胡柳陂之战.sides: Jin won a costly victory over Later Liang
battle:胡柳陂之战.note: The two armies charged back and forth at Huliupo, each losing tens of thousands; the Jin general Zhou Dewei and his son were killed in battle.

battle:中都之战.note: Li Cunxu captured the Liang general Wang Yanzhang; Li Siyuan made a long dash to strike Kaifeng, the last Liang emperor killed himself, and the Later Liang fell.

battle:灭前蜀之役.cmd: Guo Chongtao and Li Jiji vs. Wang Yan
battle:灭前蜀之役.note: 60,000 Later Tang troops entered Shu from Fengzhou and reached Chengdu in seventy days, and Wang Yan surrendered. Soon afterwards Guo Chongtao was falsely accused by eunuchs and killed.

battle:忽汗城之战.note: The Khitans first took Fuyu Fu, then besieged Huhan City; the Balhae king Dae Inseon surrendered, and Balhae, which had lasted 229 years, came to an end.

battle:晋阳之战.sides: Khitan and Shi Jingtang defeated Later Tang
battle:晋阳之战.note: Shi Jingtang rebelled at Taiyuan; 50,000 Khitan horsemen came to his aid, routed the Later Tang army and besieged it at Jin'an Fort. Zhang Jingda was killed by his own officers and the whole army surrendered to the Khitans; Shi Jingtang proclaimed himself emperor and marched south, and the Later Tang fell.

battle:白藤江之战.note: Ngô Quyền secretly planted iron-tipped stakes in the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River and lured the Southern Han fleet into the river at high tide; when the tide fell the ships were caught on the stakes. Southern Han was badly defeated, and Liu Hongcao, son of the Southern Han ruler and Prince of Jiao, was killed. The next year Ngô Quyền proclaimed himself king, and Vietnam broke free of rule by the dynasties of the Central Plains.

battle:阳城之战.cmd: Du Chongwei and Fu Yanqing vs. Yelü Deguang
battle:阳城之战.note: Surrounded and short of water at Baituanwei Village, the Jin army broke out in a strong wind under Fu Yanqing and others; the Khitans were badly beaten and Yelü Deguang fled on a camel.

battle:建州之役.note: The Wang brothers of Min were fighting a civil war; Southern Tang seized the chance to send troops and took Jianzhou in the 8th month of 945. Wang Yanzheng surrendered, and Min fell.

battle:中渡桥之降.note: Du Chongwei, leading the 100,000-strong main army of Later Jin, was surrounded at the Zhongdu Bridge over the Hutuo River and surrendered to the Khitans; Jin lost its best troops, and the same month the Khitan vanguard under Zhang Yanze broke into Kaifeng.

battle:南唐灭楚.note: As the sons of the Ma family of Chu fought one another, the Southern Tang general Bian Hao entered Changsha; the whole Ma clan was moved east to Jinling, and Chu fell. The next year Liu Yan and Wang Kui drove out the Southern Tang army.

battle:高平之战.sides: Later Zhou defeated Northern Han and Liao
battle:高平之战.cmd: Chai Rong and Zhao Kuangyin vs. Liu Chong and Yang Gun
battle:高平之战.note: Soon after Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou came to the throne, Northern Han attacked together with Liao. When Fan Aineng's right wing fled from the field, Shizong braved arrows and stones to lead the fight in person, Zhao Kuangyin and others charged, and the Han–Liao army was routed. Afterwards Fan Aineng and more than seventy other officers were executed and the Palace Army was reorganized.

battle:紫金山之战.cmd: Chai Rong vs. Liu Renshan and Zhu Yuan
battle:紫金山之战.note: Liu Renshan, the commander at Shouzhou, held out for more than a year; in 957 Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou led the army himself and routed the Southern Tang relief army at Mount Zijin, and Shouzhou surrendered. In 958 Southern Tang ceded its fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze.

battle:收复三关.note: On his northern campaign Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou took Ningzhou, Yijin Pass, Waqiao Pass, Yukou Pass and the prefectures of Mozhou and Yingzhou in forty-two days without a battle; just as he was about to advance on Youzhou he fell seriously ill and turned back.

battle:宋灭后蜀.cmd: Wang Quanbin and Liu Guangyi vs. Meng Chang
battle:宋灭后蜀.note: The Song army entered Shu in two columns, from Fengzhou and Guizhou, conquered it in sixty-six days, and Meng Chang surrendered.

battle:韶州之战.note: Pan Mei attacked Hezhou and Shaozhou. Southern Han met him with war elephants; the Song troops shot the elephants with crossbows, the elephants turned and charged their own side, and Southern Han was badly beaten. In the 2nd month of 971 the Song army entered Guangzhou and Liu Chang surrendered.

battle:采石渡江.cmd: Cao Bin and Pan Mei vs. Li Yu
battle:采石渡江.note: Using Fan Ruoshui's measurements of the width of the river, the Song army built a pontoon bridge at Caishiji and crossed the Yangtze; it besieged Jinling for nearly a year, the city fell in the 11th month of 975, and Li Yu surrendered.

battle:太原之战@979.cmd: Emperor Taizong of Song vs. Liu Jiyuan
battle:太原之战@979.note: The Song army first drove back a Liao relief army at Shiling Pass; Emperor Taizong of Song came to the walls himself to direct the assault, and Liu Jiyuan surrendered. Taizong ordered the old city of Jinyang burned.

battle:高梁河之战.cmd: Yelü Xiuge and Yelü Xiezhen vs. Emperor Taizong of Song
battle:高梁河之战.note: After destroying Northern Han the Song army pressed on to attack Youzhou but could not take it; when Liao reinforcements arrived it was badly beaten at the Gaoliang River, and Emperor Taizong of Song, wounded by an arrow, fled south in a donkey cart. From then on Song and Liao faced each other for a long time.

pass:潼关.note: The eastern gate of Guanzhong. It fell twice, in the An Lushan Rebellion and in Huang Chao's rebellion, and each time Chang'an fell with it.

pass:蒲津关.note: A Yellow River crossing joining Guanzhong and Hedong; in the Kaiyuan era the Tang cast iron oxen to anchor its pontoon bridge.

pass:武关.note: The southeastern gate of Chang'an, leading through Shangzhou to Xiangzhou and Dengzhou.

pass:大散关.note: The northern entrance of the Qinling, commanding the Chencang road (Jialing road) into Hanzhong and Shu.

pass:陇关.note: Also called Dazhen Pass, the main road over the Long Mountains; after Tibet took Longyou it became a Tang–Tibetan frontier pass.

pass:萧关.note: The northwestern gate of Guanzhong; with the Seven Passes of Yuanzhou, a key point of the frontier defense.

pass:六盘关.note: One of the "Seven Passes" of Yuanzhou (Shimen, Yizang, Zhisheng, Liupan, Shixia, Mujing and Muxia), recovered together with Yuanzhou in 849.

pass:剑门关.note: A natural fortress on the Jinniu road: "one man holding the pass can stop ten thousand".

pass:瞿塘关.note: The western mouth of the Three Gorges, the eastern gate of Shu.

pass:虎牢关.note: The eastern gate of Luoyang, commanding the main road between Bianzhou and Luoyang.

pass:天井关.note: A pass on the Taihang Xing, linking Zelu and Heyang.

pass:井陉口.note: Also called Tumen Pass, one of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, linking Hedong and Hebei (Chengde).

pass:飞狐口.note: One of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, the route from Yuzhou to Yizhou and Dingzhou.

pass:雁门关.note: Called Xixing Pass under the Tang; the northern barrier of Hedong, and later on the Song–Liao border.

pass:居庸关.note: The Jundu Xing of the Eight Passes of the Taihang; the northern gate of Youzhou.

pass:古北口.note: The main road northeast from Youzhou to the Xi and the Khitans.

pass:松亭关.note: Site of the Lulong Fortress, the main road from Pingzhou into the Xi lands.

pass:渝关.note: Also called Linyu Pass (the Yu is also written with a different character); at the western end of the Liaoxi Corridor, lost to the Khitans early in the Five Dynasties, while Zhou Dewei governed Youzhou.

pass:瓦桥关.note: Recovered by Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou in 959, who set up Xiongzhou here; with Yijin and Yukou it formed the "Three Passes", key fortresses on the Song–Liao border.

pass:益津关.note: Recovered in 959; Bazhou was set up here.

pass:大庾岭.note: One of the Five Ridges. In the Kaiyuan era Zhang Jiuling opened the Meiling road, the most important route between Lingnan and the Central Plains.

pass:玉门关.note: The Tang Yumen Pass lay east of Jinchang City in Guazhou; Xuanzang left through it on his journey west.

pass:阳关.note: The pass southwest of Shazhou onto the Southern Route of the Western Regions: "west of Yang Pass you will meet no old friends".

pass:铁门关.note: A gorge pass on the road from Karasahr to Kucha.

pass:石堡城.note: A fortress fought over again and again by Tang and Tibet. Geshu Han took it in 749 at a cost of tens of thousands of casualties; it was later lost again.

event:范阳起兵.note: Under the pretext of "punishing Yang Guozhong", An Lushan marched south from Fanyang with 150,000 men (claimed as 200,000) from his own troops and Tongra, Xi, Khitan and Shiwei soldiers. The An Lushan Rebellion had begun.

event:马嵬驿之变.note: Fleeing west, Emperor Xuanzong reached Mawei Station, where the Palace Army mutinied, killed Yang Guozhong and forced Xuanzong to have Yang Guifei strangled. The crown prince Li Heng went north, while Xuanzong went on to Shu.

event:灵武即位.note: The crown prince Li Heng took the throne at Lingwu (Emperor Suzong), honored Xuanzong as Retired Emperor, and relied on the Shuofang army to put down the rebellion.

event:杜甫草堂.note: Living as a refugee in Chengdu, Du Fu built a thatched cottage by the Huanhua Stream, where he wrote "My Thatched Hut Torn by the Autumn Wind", "Good Rain on a Spring Night" and other poems.

event:陆羽著《茶经》.old: Lu Yu writes The Classic of Tea
event:陆羽著《茶经》.note: Living as a recluse by the Tiao Stream in Huzhou, Lu Yu wrote The Classic of Tea, and tea drinking spread across the country; in 793 the Tang began to tax tea.

event:两税法.note: The chief minister Yang Yan introduced the Two-Tax Law, levied in summer and autumn according to household grade and landholding, in place of the zu-yong-diao system: a major turning point in China's tax system.

event:景教碑.note: The Stele of the Propagation of the Luminous Religion of Daqin in China stood at the Daqin Monastery in the Yining Ward of Chang'an. It records 150 years of the Luminous Religion (Nestorian Christianity) in China.

event:点苍山会盟.note: The Tang envoy Cui Zuoshi and the Nanzhao king Yimouxun swore a covenant at the shrine on the Diancang Mountains; Nanzhao broke with Tibet and returned to Tang allegiance.

event:永州八记.note: After the failure of the Yongzhen Reform, Liu Zongyuan spent ten years banished as adjutant of Yongzhou, where he wrote the Eight Records of Yongzhou and "The Snake Catcher".

event:江州司马.note: Banished as adjutant of Jiangzhou, Bai Juyi wrote "Song of the Pipa" and built a thatched hall on Mount Lu.

event:韩愈贬潮州.note: When Emperor Xianzong had the Buddha's bone from Famen Temple brought into the palace, Han Yu submitted his "Memorial on the Buddha's Bone" and was demoted to prefect of Chaozhou, where he founded schools and drove off the crocodiles; the local hills and rivers were later all named "Han" after him.

event:唐蕃会盟碑.note: Tang and Tibet swore treaties first at Chang'an and then at Rasa (the Treaty of Changqing), agreeing that "each shall keep to its own territory and neither shall invade the other"; the text was carved in Chinese and Tibetan in front of the Jokhang Temple.

event:清海镇.note: The Silla man Jang Bogo set up the Cheonghae Garrison on Wando, controlling the Yellow Sea trade route and sailing between Dengzhou, Chuzhou and Hakata in Japan.

event:维州受降.note: Xidamou, the Tibetan deputy commander at Weizhou, surrendered the city to Li Deyu, military governor of Xichuan; the chief minister Niu Sengru ordered it returned on the grounds of the treaty, and Xidamou and his men were killed by the Tibetans. It became a famous case in the factional struggle between Niu and Li.

event:甘露之变.note: Emperor Wenzong plotted with Li Xun and Zheng Zhu to kill the eunuchs, luring Qiu Shiliang with the pretext of viewing "sweet dew"; the plot leaked, and the eunuchs led the Shence Army in slaughtering more than a thousand court officials, clerks, guards and townspeople. After this the eunuchs were more overbearing than ever.

event:圆仁入唐.note: The Japanese monk Ennin came to Tang China with the last Japanese embassy to the Tang, made pilgrimages to Mount Wutai and Chang'an, lived through the Huichang persecution of Buddhism, and returned home with the help of the Silla communities in Chuzhou and Dengzhou. He wrote the Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law.

event:会昌灭佛.note: Emperor Wuzong ordered more than 4,600 monasteries destroyed and more than 260,000 monks and nuns returned to lay life. Mount Wutai was then a holy place of Buddhism; Ennin had made a pilgrimage there five years earlier.

event:裘甫起事.note: Qiu Fu rose in Zhedong with up to 30,000 followers and was put down by Wang Shi; it was the prelude to the popular risings of the late Tang.

event:《金刚经》刻本.note: The Diamond Sutra printed in Xiantong 9 (868), found in the Dunhuang Library Cave, is the earliest surviving woodblock print with a precise date. The cave was sealed around the early 11th century and discovered in 1900; it yielded more than 50,000 documents.

event:法门寺地宫.note: After Emperor Yizong had the Buddha's finger relic brought to the court, Emperor Xizong sealed the crypt in 874; its excavation in 1987 uncovered Tang palace gold and silver ware, "secret-color" porcelain and other treasures.

event:黄巢起事.note: Wang Xianzhi rose at Changyuan and Huang Chao at Yuanqu; starving people joined them, and they fought their way across Shandong, Henan and Huainan.

event:长沙窑.note: The Changsha kilns pioneered underglaze painting; their wares were shipped through Yangzhou and Guangzhou to West Asia and Southeast Asia, and more than 50,000 pieces were recovered from the Batu Hitam (Belitung) shipwreck.

event:越窑秘色瓷.note: Yue ware celadon was "like jade, like ice"; in the late Tang it was called "secret color", and the Qian family of Wuyue sent it as tribute. Fourteen pieces were found in the crypt of Famen Temple.

event:邢窑白瓷.note: Xing ware white porcelain was "like silver, like snow"; together with Yue ware it made up "celadon in the south, white in the north".

event:长安毁城.note: Zhu Quanzhong forced Emperor Zhaozong to move the capital to Luoyang and pulled down the palaces and houses of Chang'an, floating the timber down the Wei and Yellow rivers to Luoyang. Chang'an was never a capital again.

event:白马驿之祸.note: At Baima Station Zhu Quanzhong killed Pei Shu and more than thirty other court officials and threw their bodies into the Yellow River, to turn the "pure stream" into a "muddy stream".

event:捍海石塘.note: Qian Liu built a seawall of stones packed in bamboo cages to protect the city of Hangzhou and its farmland (the legend of "King Qian shooting the tide").

event:契丹大字.note: Yelü Abaoji had the Khitan large script created on the model of Chinese characters; a little later Yelü Diela created the Khitan small script.

event:冯道刻九经.old: Feng Dao prints the Nine Classics
event:冯道刻九经.note: Feng Dao, chief minister of Later Tang, asked for the Nine Classics to be printed from the text of the Tang Kaicheng Stone Classics; the work took twenty-two years under four dynasties and began the large-scale woodblock printing of the Confucian classics.

event:《花间集》.note: Zhao Chongzuo of Later Shu compiled Among the Flowers, the earliest anthology of ci lyrics by literati; the Later Shu chief minister Wu Zhaoyi paid to have the Nine Classics and other books printed.

event:梁山泊.note: The Yellow River broke its banks at Huazhou and flooded the five prefectures of Kaifeng, Caozhou, Shanzhou, Puzhou and Yunzhou, gathering around Mount Liang into a great marsh: Liangshan Marsh.

event:陈桥兵变.note: Sent north to resist Liao and Northern Han, Zhao Kuangyin reached Chenqiao Station, where his men draped a yellow robe on him; he led the army back to Kaifeng, Emperor Gong of Later Zhou abdicated in his favor, and the Song dynasty was founded.

people:沙陀@755.note: A branch of the Western Turks, originally living around Jinman Zhou near Beiting; in 808 they led their people east and submitted to the Tang.

people:沙陀@808.note: After moving east in 808 they were settled at Yanzhou, then moved to Daibei (around Shenwuchuan in today's northern Shanxi). Their chief Zhuye Chixin was given the name Li Guochang; his son Li Keyong built up his dominance in Hedong. The Later Tang, Later Jin and Later Han all came from the Shatuo.

people:党项.note: A Qiang people originally living in Qinghai and northwestern Sichuan. Pressed by Tibet, they moved into the area of Qingzhou, Xiazhou and Yinzhou and divided into the Pingxia, Dongshan and other groups. The Tuoba clan of the Pingxia group later founded Western Xia.

people:退浑.note: That is, the Tuyuhun. After their state fell in 663 their people moved into Tang territory; in the late Tang they lived scattered across Daibei and Hedong, mixed with the Shatuo and the Tatars.

people:吐谷浑.note: After 663 the Tuyuhun lands were annexed by Tibet, and their people became Tibetan subjects.

people:鞑靼.note: Originally the Shiwei–Tatar tribes under Turkic and Uyghur rule; after the fall of the Uyghurs they moved south into the Yin Mountains. Li Keyong took refuge with the Tatars after his defeat in 880.

people:嗢末.note: The bonded tribes of the Tibetans during their rule of Hexi and Longyou. After Tibet collapsed they rose around 861 and gathered around Liangzhou.

people:仲云.note: A tribe of the Southern Mountains (Altyn-Tagh) who called themselves descendants of the Lesser Yuezhi; they fought and made peace with Guiyi Jun by turns.

people:蒙兀室韦.note: Lived east of the Wangjian River (Argun); ancestors of the Mongols.

people:骨利干.note: Lived north of the Northern Sea (Lake Baikal); they bred fine horses and were known for their "long days and short nights".

people:东女国.note: A people of the western Sichuan plateau ruled by a queen; they submitted to the Tang in 793.

people:两林蛮.note: A people south of the Dadu River (the Eastern tribes) who wavered between Tang and Nanzhao.

people:牂牁蛮.note: A people of today's central Guizhou; the Tang set up loose-rein prefectures for them, and they often sent tribute missions.

people:溪洞诸蛮.note: The peoples of the Five Streams region (today's western Hunan and eastern Guizhou). In the Five Dynasties the Peng family of Xizhou rose to power; it fought Chu at Xizhou in 939–940, and in 940 a bronze pillar was set up to seal the peace.

people:黄洞蛮.note: The Huang, Nong and other clans southwest of Yongzhou, who rose repeatedly in the later Tang; Nong Zhigao of the Song came from them.

people:黎.note: The Li peoples (俚 and 黎) of central Hainan.

people:乌蛮.note: The Wuman tribes on the eastern border of Nanzhao (today's northeastern Yunnan and western Guizhou).

people:样磨.note: One of the tribes that made up the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

region:燕云十六州.old: Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun
region:燕云十六州.mod: today's Beijing, northern Tianjin, northern Hebei and northern Shanxi

g.山前七州: Seven prefectures south of the mountains
g.山后九州: Nine prefectures north of the mountains
g.瀛莫 959 归周: Ying and Mo, to Later Zhou in 959

region:燕云十六州.note:
In 936 Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, rose against the Later Tang and asked the Khitans for help, promising them "the whole of Lulong and the prefectures north of Yanmen Pass" and agreeing to be their subject and "son emperor"; the handover was completed in 938 (Tianfu 3 of Later Jin).
Seven prefectures south of the mountains (southeast of the northern branch of the Taihang Mountains): Youzhou (today's Beijing), Jizhou (Jizhou, Tianjin), Yingzhou (Hejian, Hebei), Mozhou (Renqiu, Hebei), Zhuozhou (Zhuozhou, Hebei), Tanzhou (Miyun, Beijing), Shunzhou (Shunyi, Beijing).
Nine prefectures north of the mountains (northwest of the mountains): Xinzhou (Zhuolu, Hebei), Guizhou (Huailai, Hebei), Ruzhou (Yanqing, Beijing), Wuzhou (Xuanhua, Zhangjiakou, Hebei), Yunzhou (Datong, Shanxi), Yingzhou (Ying County, Shanxi), Huanzhou (east of Shuozhou, Shanxi), Shuozhou (Shuozhou, Shanxi), Yuzhou (Yu County, Hebei).
The Central Plains thus lost the barrier of the Yan Mountains, the Great Wall and Yanmen, and Khitan cavalry could ride straight down onto the North China Plain. Liao made Youzhou Youdu Fu (Southern Capital) in 938, and later made Yunzhou its Western Capital in 1044.
In 959 Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou campaigned north and recovered Yingzhou and Mozhou and the three passes of Waqiao, Yijin and Yukou, setting up Xiongzhou and Bazhou; after Emperor Taizong of Song's defeat at the Gaoliang River in 979, the Northern Song never truly recovered the remaining prefectures (in 1123 it bought back Yanjing and other places from Jin, only to lose them again in 1125).
Huanzhou was created in Tiancheng 1 (926) of Later Tang, with its seat at Huanqing County; it was abolished after passing to Liao.

capital:邺城（安庆绪）.note: In the 10th month of 757 An Qingxu abandoned Luoyang and went north to hold Ye Commandery (Xiangzhou), which he renamed Ancheng Fu; in the winter of 758 nine military governors besieged Yecheng, and in the 3rd month of 759 Shi Siming came to its relief, broke the siege and soon afterwards killed An Qingxu.

capital:蔡州（秦宗权）.note: Qin Zongquan proclaimed himself emperor at Caizhou in 885 and sent his officers out to plunder in all directions; in 887 he was badly defeated at Bianxiao Village outside Bianzhou, in 888 his officer Shen Cong seized him, and the next year he was sent to Chang'an and beheaded.

battle:汴州之战.sides: Tang (allied fanzhen) defeated Li Lingyao and Weibo
battle:汴州之战.cmd: Li Zhongchen and Ma Sui vs. Li Lingyao and Tian Yue
battle:汴州之战.note: Li Lingyao, acting military governor of Biansong, revolted at Bianzhou, and Tian Chengsi of Weibo sent his nephew Tian Yue to help him; troops of several fanzhen, among them Li Zhongchen of Huaixi and Ma Sui of Heyang, routed Tian Yue under the walls of Bianzhou and broke into the city, and Li Lingyao fled and was captured. Li Zhengji of Ziqing took the chance to seize the five prefectures of Caozhou, Puzhou, Xuzhou, Yanzhou and Yunzhou, changing the balance of power in Henan.

battle:神川之战.note: After Nanzhao swore its covenant with the Tang on the Diancang Mountains, Yimouxun pretended to send troops to help Tibet and instead fell on Shenchuan on the Jinsha River, routing the Tibetans and cutting the iron bridge; he received the submission of more than 100,000 tribespeople under Tibetan control and took sixteen towns, Tieqiao City among them. From then on Nanzhao joined the Tang against Tibet.

battle:交州之陷.cmd: Yang Sijin and Duan Qiuqian vs. Cai Xi
battle:交州之陷.note: Nanzhao, joined by local anti-Tang forces, besieged Giao Châu; Cai Xi, Protector-General of Annan, was cut off from relief; when the city fell he fought on and drowned. His aide Fan Chuo escaped across the river and later wrote the Manshu, an account of Nanzhao's land and customs. The Tang army fell back to Haimen (around modern Hepu, Guangxi), and Nanzhao held Annan for three years.

battle:边孝村之战.sides: Xuanwu, Yicheng, Tianping and Taining defeated Qin Zongquan
battle:边孝村之战.cmd: Zhu Quanzhong, Zhu Xuan and Zhu Jin vs. Qin Zongquan
battle:边孝村之战.note: Qin Zongquan massed his troops to besiege Bianzhou; Zhu Quanzhong, joined by Zhu Xuan of Yunzhou and Zhu Jin of Yanzhou, routed the Cai army at Bianxiao Village in the northern outskirts of Bianzhou, taking more than 20,000 heads. Qin Zongquan never recovered: Luoyang, Heyang, Xuzhou, Ruzhou, Zhengzhou, Shanzhou and the other places he held were abandoned one after another, and the next year his officers seized him and handed him over. From then on Zhu Quanzhong was master of Henan.

battle:宣州之战.note: Sun Ru, a former officer of Qin Zongquan, crossed the Yangtze with several hundred thousand men and fought Yang Xingmi for Huainan and Jiangnan, laying a long siege to Xuanzhou; in 892 an epidemic broke out in Sun Ru's army, and Yang Xingmi struck, capturing and beheading Sun Ru. The rest of Sun Ru's army went south under Liu Jianfeng and Ma Yin and later seized Hunan. Yang Xingmi thereby held Huainan and laid the foundation of the state of Wu.

battle:李克用讨王行瑜.old: Li Keyong's campaign against Wang Xingyu
battle:李克用讨王行瑜.note: Wang Xingyu, Li Maozhen and Han Jian led troops into Chang'an, killed chief ministers on their own authority and plotted to depose Emperor Zhaozong. Li Keyong led the Hedong army south against them, beat the Binning army again and again at Liyuan Stockade and took Binzhou; Wang Xingyu was killed by his own men as he fled. Li Keyong was invested as Prince of Jin, but once he withdrew he could not control Guanzhong, and the court remained in the grip of Fengxiang and Huazhou.

battle:鸡踪桥之战.cmd: Meng Zhixiang and Zhao Tingyin vs. Dong Zhang
battle:鸡踪桥之战.note: Dong Zhang led the Dongchuan army in a surprise attack on Xichuan; Meng Zhixiang met him in person with a large army and routed the Dongchuan troops at Jizong Bridge in Hanzhou. Dong Zhang fled back to Zizhou and was killed by his own men, and Meng Zhixiang gained all the lands of the two Chuan; two years later he proclaimed himself emperor and founded Later Shu.

battle:夏州之战.cmd: Li Yichao vs. An Congjin and Yao Yanchou
battle:夏州之战.note: When Li Renfu, military governor of Dingnan, died, his son Li Yichao set himself up; Emperor Mingzong of Later Tang transferred An Congjin to Xiazhou and sent a large army to escort him there. Li Yichao held out in Tongwan City, whose walls were too strong to storm, while the Tangut tribes cut the supply lines; after more than a hundred days the Tang army withdrew with nothing to show for it. From then on the Dingnan Jun held Yinzhou, Xiazhou and its other prefectures as a hereditary domain, the foundation on which the Western Xia state was later built.

battle:泽州之战.cmd: Zhao Kuangyin and Shi Shouxin vs. Li Yun
battle:泽州之战.note: Li Yun, the Later Zhou military governor of Zhaoyi, refused to accept the Song, rose at Luzhou and allied with Northern Han; Emperor Taizu of Song took the field in person. Shi Shouxin and others routed Li Yun south of Zezhou and besieged the city; when it fell, Li Yun burned himself to death. Emperor Taizu then put down Li Chongjin at Yangzhou, and the new dynasty was essentially secure.

battle:三江口之战.cmd: Murong Yanzhao and Li Chuyun vs. the Hunan army
battle:三江口之战.note: On the pretext of putting down Zhang Wenbiao, the Song army asked for passage through Jingnan and took over Jingnan from the Gao family on its way; it then went south into Hunan, routed the Hunan fleet at Sanjiangkou at the mouth of Lake Dongting, took Yuezhou and occupied Langzhou. Zhou Baoquan was captured, Jinghu passed to the Song, and the Song now commanded the middle Yangtze.

event:河朔复叛.note: Emperor Muzong mishandled Hebei: the Youzhou army imprisoned its newly appointed military governor Zhang Hongjing and set up Zhu Kerong; the Chengde army killed Tian Hongzheng and made Wang Tingcou acting military governor; the next year Shi Xiancheng took over Weibo. The gains of Emperor Xianzong's "Yuanhe Restoration" were almost all lost within a year.

event:吴越纳土.note: Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, came to court at Kaifeng and handed over the thirteen prefectures and one jun under his rule, "surrendering his lands to the Song". The Qian family, five rulers over three generations, had held Liangzhe for more than seventy years, keeping their state safe and their people at peace and building the seawall against the tides, and Hangzhou prospered as a result.

route:黄巢转战.mod: Heze, Shandong – Guangzhou, Guangdong – Xi'an, Shaanxi – Laiwu District, Jinan, Shandong
route:黄巢转战.note: In Qianfu 2 (875) Huang Chao rose at Yuanqu in support of Wang Xianzhi and fought his way through Shandong, Henan and Huainan. After Wang Xianzhi was defeated and killed in 878, Huang Chao took the title Heaven-Storming General, crossed the Yangtze and went south, cutting a mountain road of seven hundred li over the Xianxia Range into Fujian, and in the 9th month of 879 he took Guangzhou. With disease spreading in his army he turned back north through Guizhou and Tanzhou to Jiangling; checked at Jingmen, he went east through Raozhou, Xinzhou and other prefectures, crossed the Yangtze at Caishi in the 7th month of 880 and the Huai in the 9th month, took Luoyang in the 11th month, and in the 12th month broke through Tong Pass and entered Chang'an. Driven out of Chang'an in 883, he went east to Caizhou and besieged Chenzhou for nearly three hundred days; he was defeated in 884 and died in the 6th month at Langhu Valley near Mount Tai.
